seo.title: How to Build a CLI Tool with Bun | Full Stack Guide
seo.description: Build a fast CLI tool using Bun's native APIs for file I/O, argument parsing, and HTTP requests, then publish it to npm as a standalone executable.

introduction: Bun makes CLI tools absurdly fast to build. No bundler config, no transpiler setup — just TypeScript that runs natively with built-in file I/O, an HTTP client, and sub-millisecond startup times. This guide covers building a practical CLI tool from argument parsing to npm publishing, using only Bun's native APIs.

prerequisites.name: Bun 1.1+
prerequisites.description: Install Bun, the all-in-one JavaScript runtime with native TypeScript support and built-in APIs for file, shell, and network operations.

prerequisites.name: npm Account
prerequisites.description: You need an npm account to publish your CLI tool as a package that others can install globally.

prerequisites.name: Basic TypeScript Knowledge
prerequisites.description: Familiarity with TypeScript types, async/await, and module imports.

steps.title: Initialize the Bun Project
steps.description: Create a new directory and initialize it with bun init. This generates a package.json and tsconfig.json tuned for Bun's runtime. Set the bin field in package.json so npm knows which file to run when your CLI command is invoked.

code_snippet.code:
mkdir my-cli && cd my-cli
bun init

# Create the CLI entry point
mkdir -p src
touch src/index.ts

tips: Bun's init sets target to 'bun' in tsconfig.json, enabling Bun-specific type definitions automatically.
Add the shebang #!/usr/bin/env bun at the top of your entry file so it runs with Bun when invoked directly.

steps.title: Parse Arguments and Build the Command Router
steps.description: Build argument parsing using Bun's native util.parseArgs (from Node.js compatibility) or roll a lightweight parser with process.argv. Define your CLI's commands and flags, then route to the correct handler. This pattern scales well — each command is a separate function that receives parsed options.
tips: Use Bun.argv instead of process.argv — same data, but Bun.argv is typed and slightly faster.
Lazy-import command handlers so the CLI starts instantly even with many commands.

steps.title: Use Bun's Native File APIs for I/O Operations
steps.description: Implement your commands using Bun.file() and Bun.write() for file operations. These APIs are significantly faster than Node's fs module because they use system calls directly. Bun.file() returns a BunFile that supports .text(), .json(), .arrayBuffer(), and streaming reads.
tips: Bun.write() accepts strings, Uint8Arrays, Blobs, or Response objects — pipe HTTP responses directly to disk.
Use Bun.file(path).exists() instead of fs.access() — it's cleaner and returns a boolean.

steps.title: Add a Local Dev Server with Bun.serve
steps.description: Build a serve command using Bun.serve() to start a local HTTP server that serves your generated files. Bun.serve is built on uWebSockets and handles thousands of concurrent connections. Add basic MIME type detection and directory listing for a complete local development experience.
tips: Bun.serve returns a Server object — call server.stop() in cleanup code or signal handlers.
Bun.file() streams large files automatically instead of buffering them in memory.

steps.title: Add Colored Output and Progress Indicators
steps.description: Make your CLI output professional with ANSI color codes and a simple spinner for long-running operations. Bun supports ANSI escape sequences natively in the terminal. Build a small utility module for consistent styling across all commands.
tips: Respect the NO_COLOR environment variable (https://no-color.org/) — some users and CI systems disable color output.
Keep spinner frames as Unicode braille characters — they render in all modern terminals.

steps.title: Configure package.json and Publish to npm
steps.description: Set up your package.json with the correct bin field, files whitelist, and type declarations. Use bun build --compile to produce a standalone binary for users who don't have Bun installed, or publish the TypeScript source for Bun users. Run npm publish to push your CLI to the registry.
tips: Use bun build --compile to produce a single executable binary that includes the Bun runtime — no dependencies needed.
Set the files field to only include src/ so you don't ship test files or config to npm.
Test your CLI locally with 'bun link' before publishing to npm.

next_steps: Add interactive prompts using Bun's built-in readline or the prompts package for guided setup flows.
Write tests with Bun's built-in test runner using bun:test for fast, zero-config testing.
Add a plugin system that loads commands from node_modules or local directories.
Set up GitHub Actions to auto-publish to npm on tagged releases.
